questions.stem: Identify the improvement: 'The committee ARE meeting tomorrow to discuss the agenda.' The underlined word is: ARE
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'The committee' functions as a collective noun acting as a single unit. In Indian/SSC English, collective nouns take singular verbs: 'The committee IS meeting'. 'Are' is used for plural subjects — wrong here.

questions.stem: She insisted on ME GOING to the party without her permission. The underlined part is: ME GOING
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a pronoun precedes a gerund (-ing form used as noun), the pronoun must be in the possessive case. 'My going' — not 'me going'. Rule: possessive + gerund (not objective pronoun + gerund). Common in formal/written English.

questions.stem: Neither of the candidates WERE found suitable for the post. The underlined word is: WERE
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Neither' is a singular indefinite pronoun → takes a singular verb. 'Neither of the candidates WAS found suitable.' The 'of the candidates' phrase is a prepositional modifier and does not change the subject's number.

questions.stem: He is THE MOST TALLEST player in the team. The underlined part is: THE MOST TALLEST
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Tallest' is already a superlative (-est form); adding 'most' is a double superlative — a grammatical error. The correct form is 'the tallest'. Rule: never use 'most' + '-est' form together.

questions.stem: The news of his promotion WERE received with great joy by all. The underlined word is: WERE
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'News' is an uncountable noun that takes a singular verb even though it ends in 's'. The subject is 'The news', which is singular → 'was received'. Similarly: 'physics is', 'mathematics is', 'economics is'.

questions.stem: No sooner did he leave the office WHEN it started raining. The underlined word is: WHEN
questions.explanation: A is correct. The fixed correlative expression is 'No sooner... THAN' (not 'when' or 'then'). Similarly: 'Hardly/Scarcely... when/before' and 'No sooner... than'. These are frequently tested SSC pattern errors.

questions.stem: He works HARD AND HONEST in his profession. The underlined part is: HARD AND HONEST
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Works' is a verb, so it needs adverbs to describe it. 'Hard' is already an adverb (no change needed); 'honest' is an adjective and must become 'honestly' to function as an adverb. Parallel structure: adverb + adverb → 'hard and honestly'.

questions.stem: It is I who IS responsible for this mistake. The underlined word is: IS
questions.explanation: C is correct. The relative pronoun 'who' refers back to 'I' (first person singular). The verb must agree with 'I' → 'am'. Correct sentence: 'It is I who AM responsible for this mistake.' This is a subtle subject-verb agreement trap.

questions.stem: The Principal along with the teachers HAVE signed the petition. The underlined word is: HAVE
questions.explanation: A is correct. When a singular subject is followed by 'along with / together with / as well as / in addition to', the verb agrees with the main (singular) subject — not with the phrase that follows. 'The Principal' is singular → 'has'. This is different from 'and', which creates a plural compound subject.

questions.stem: Had he WORKED harder, he would have passed the examination. The underlined word is: WORKED
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Had he worked harder...' is a valid inverted third conditional (past perfect in the 'if' clause, with 'if' omitted and the subject-auxiliary inverted). Correct form: 'Had + subject + past participle → would have + past participle'. The sentence is already grammatically perfect. This tests whether students recognise correct inversion and mark 'No improvement'.
